Esther 1.audience: Esther was written for Jews living under Persian rule, many of them outside the land of Israel. It is set at Shushan, a royal capital of the Persian empire, under King Ahasuerus, usually identified with Xerxes I (486–465 BC).

culture.title: An empire of 127 provinces
culture.text: Ahasuerus ruled from India to Ethiopia (Cush) over 127 provinces. The Greek historian Herodotus describes Xerxes' empire stretching across the same regions.

culture.title: Royal banquets
culture.text: Persian kings held lavish feasts in palace gardens, with couches of gold and silver on mosaic pavements, and wine served in gold vessels "according to the state of the king."

culture.title: Laws that cannot be changed
culture.text: A decree of the king written "among the laws of the Persians and the Medes" could not be altered (also Daniel 6:8).

Esther 2.audience: Mordecai is introduced as a Benjamite descended from Kish, whose family had been taken into exile with King Jeconiah (Esther 2:5–6). Readers would know these as Jews who stayed in Persia rather than return.

culture.title: Twelve months of preparation
culture.text: Each young woman was prepared for twelve months—six with oil of myrrh and six with perfumes and ointments—before going to the king.

culture.title: Two names
culture.text: Esther's Hebrew name is Hadassah, ‘myrtle.’ Jews in exile often had a second name used in the foreign culture, as Daniel and his friends did (Daniel 1:7).

culture.title: The king's gate
culture.text: Mordecai sits "in the king's gate," where royal officials worked. From there he uncovers a plot against the king.

Esther 3.audience: Haman is called "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1). Readers would recall Agag, king of the Amalekites, Israel's ancient enemy, whom Saul the son of Kish had spared (1 Samuel 15:8).

culture.title: Bowing to officials
culture.text: Persian court custom required bowing before high officials. Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman.

culture.title: Casting Pur
culture.text: Haman casts pur (lots) to choose the day for destroying the Jews. A small clay die inscribed as a pur has been found from ancient Assyria. The feast of Purim is named after these lots (Esther 9:26).

culture.title: The royal signet
culture.text: The king gives Haman his signet ring, which sealed decrees with royal authority. Persian couriers then carried the decree to every province.

Esther 4.audience: The Jews in every province mourn with fasting, weeping, and sackcloth (Esther 4:3). Readers would hear Mordecai's question to Esther: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14).

culture.title: No sackcloth at the gate
culture.text: No one could enter the king's gate dressed in sackcloth, so Mordecai mourns outside it.

culture.title: Approaching the king uninvited
culture.text: Anyone who came to the king in the inner court without being called was put to death unless the king held out the golden sceptre. Herodotus also describes the Persian king's protected seclusion.

Esther 5.audience: Esther approaches the king after three days of fasting. Readers would see her invite the king and Haman to two banquets before making her request.

culture.title: Up to half the kingdom
culture.text: "It shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom" was a royal expression of generosity, also used by Herod (Mark 6:23).

culture.title: A gallows fifty cubits high
culture.text: Haman builds a gallows (a stake or pole) fifty cubits—about 75 feet—high. Persians executed by impaling or hanging on a pole.

Esther 6.audience: Readers would see the king, unable to sleep, have the royal chronicles read to him and discover that Mordecai was never rewarded.

culture.title: Royal chronicles
culture.text: Persian kings kept records of events and of those who served them. Herodotus says Xerxes recorded the names of men who did him service.

culture.title: Honor by royal robe and horse
culture.text: Wearing the king's own robe and riding his horse with a royal crown, led through the city by a noble, was the highest public honor.

Esther 7.audience: Esther reveals Haman's plot at her second banquet. Readers would see Haman hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.

culture.title: Reclining at a banquet
culture.text: Persians reclined on couches to eat. Haman falls on the couch where Esther is reclining to beg for his life, and the king takes it as an assault.

culture.title: Covering the condemned's face
culture.text: As soon as the king speaks, "they covered Haman's face"—a sign that he was condemned.

Esther 8.audience: A new decree allows the Jews to defend themselves. Readers would see it written in every province's script and language, and in the Jews' own (Esther 8:9).

culture.title: Couriers on royal horses
culture.text: Letters are sent by riders on swift horses and mules. Herodotus admired the Persian royal postal system, with relays of riders across the empire.

culture.title: Royal colors
culture.text: Mordecai leaves the king's presence in royal apparel of blue and white, with a great gold crown and a garment of fine linen and purple.

Esther 9.audience: The days of Purim on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar are established here (Esther 9:21). Jewish communities still keep Purim by reading Esther aloud.

culture.title: Not taking the spoil
culture.text: Three times the text notes that the Jews "laid not their hand on the prey" (Esther 9:10, 15–16).

culture.title: Gifts and portions
culture.text: Purim is kept with feasting, joy, "sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor."

Esther 10.audience: The book ends with Mordecai "next unto king Ahasuerus" and his deeds recorded in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia (Esther 10:2–3).

culture.title: Tribute from the isles
culture.text: Ahasuerus lays a tribute on the land and the isles of the sea—the coastlands and islands under Persian rule.
